notes: \cpara{Opens with an analogy: the wish to fly was not irrational; only the ``magic potions'' were. The potions have a real history. European folklore and early modern witch trials described a ``flying ointment'' said to let witches fly (Wikipedia, ``Flying ointment'').}

\cpara{A hypothetical scan, hedged ``maybe, maybe not'': the author's brain at a shuttle launch might look like a devout Christian's at a nativity scene. It is offered as a possibility, not a finding.}
\cpara{Imagines the reply the post will argue against: ``space travel is your religion!''}
\cpara{The answer: a shared feeling does not put two things in one category. The airplane comparison makes the point directly. That some people once sought flight by magic does not taint flying.}
\cpara{Denies that the feeling is a substitute for religion, and names the opposing view ``theomorphism'': the assumption that every nonbeliever has a hole that wants filling.}

\cpara{Concedes that some atheists do try to fill a religion-shaped hole, and judges the results ``invariably awful.'' The post names no example, here or later, so the reader cannot check the verdict.}
\cpara{Names the category: ``hymns to the nonexistence of God.''}
\cpara{Repeats the verdict of two paragraphs earlier as a rule without exceptions. The only sample line, ``Hail, oh unintelligent universe,'' is the post's own.}

\cpara{Explains the badness by motive: such writers have ``no motivation for writing the hymn except a vague feeling that since churches have hymns, they ought to have one too.'' This is a claim about the motives of every such writer, and none is named.}

\clogic{The tradition the post praises also imitates. Isaac Watts, credited by many, Wikipedia says, with introducing hymns to the English churches, titled a 1719 psalter \textsc{Psalms of David: Imitated in the Language of the New Testament}. So imitation by itself cannot be what makes a hymn bad; the post's other reason, the writer's motive, has to carry the claim.}
\cpara{Credits the quality of religious hymns to strong feeling, honest writing and careful craft, hedged with ``(often).''}
\cpara{Asks the question the next paragraphs answer.}

\cpara{States the post's test: would the song, art or ritual still make sense if religion had never existed? The test asks about a world no one can observe, so each verdict rests on the author's judgment of what that world would contain.}

\cpara{Applies the test: hymns to the nonexistence of God fail it, atheistic weddings pass, provided no one lectures on God's nonexistence. Practice fits this line. Humanist weddings had been legal in Scotland since 2005, and in 2017 the Humanist Society Scotland ``conducted more weddings than the Church of Scotland or the Scottish Catholic Church'' (Wikipedia, ``Humanist Society Scotland'').}
\cpara{Applies the test to the shuttle launch: people would still weep at one.}

\cpara{Returns to the hypothetical scan. Even if it showed ``religion''-associated areas lighting up, the author would not call the feeling a substitute, because the author expects the same response in a world without religion. The conclusion is hedged with ``I expect.''}
\cpara{Answers the question: a good atheistic hymn is a song about anything worth singing about that is not religious.}

\cpara{Warns against the opposite error, avoiding everything that resembles religion, with a pointer to ``Reversed Stupidity Is Not Intelligence.'' The Sun line adapts Robert Pirsig, whom that post quotes: ``The world's greatest fool may say the Sun is shining, but that doesn't make it dark out.''}
\cpara{Restates the conclusion: tears at a launch mean caring bound to the real world, not a hole left by religion.}

\cpara{Makes two claims about believers in general: that their ``outward fervor'' compensates for ``inner uncertainty,'' and that belief shared by everyone would end ``the specialness of being one of the elect.'' Both are stated as fact, without evidence. The first has general support. McGregor and colleagues (2001) found that people made to feel uncertain ``masked the uncertainty with more extreme conviction about social issues.'' As its abstract describes it, that study concerns social issues and group bias, not religious belief, and the post offers nothing on religious belief.}
\cpara{Contrasts: awe at the shuttle survives seeing it, and survives everyone else believing in it.}

\cpara{Ends on the claim that humanity ``actually exists.'' The word ``humanism'' appears only in the title. The post answers the title's question for the author's own awe at space launches, not for humanism as an organized movement, whose first manifesto (1933) described a new religion and called humanism ``the religion of the future'' (Wikipedia, ``Humanist Manifesto I'').}
